through_lines.1: Udaypur today, the names and memories it keeps, and what the records do and do not establish about Udayāditya's foundation.
through_lines.10: Udaypur across its masters: the V.S. 1220 stone naming the Caulukya Kumārapāla and his mahāsādhanika at Udaypur (U1); Naravarman's frayed east, the mahākumāras at Vidisha, Caulukya governors, Vindhyavarman's return; Devapāla residing at Udayapura (1232), Iltutmish at Bhilsa, three-sided pressure, 1305; the Sam. 1366 title, the mosque of 1336–38 and the temple left in worship, the survival legends tested; temples turned to mosques at Vidisha, Ujjain and Dhār, Udayeśvara the exception; the Malwa sultans' Bhilsa and the 1488 mosque; Sarkar Chanderi, the translated farman, the Shahi Masjid of A.H. 1041 and the qāzī's claim (U7); Aurangzeb at Bhilsa in 1682, at Udaypur only in legend; Afghans and Marathas to Scindia by 1775; the brass cover (HELD, RR-2); Gwalior's district to Madhya Pradesh; the famine of 1899–1900 and the feeder road of 1905; political demotion dated step by step, economic decline undatable, the Gazetteer's 'once a place of considerable importance' into Chapter 11.
through_lines.11: Made known and protected in pieces: Beglar's report (1871–72) carrying the Aurangzeb legend, corrected from the inscriptions in Cunningham's (1874–77); the bedi and the eight-shrine plan as fixtures; the records in the Survey's files; Kramrisch's 1946 model resting on the reports; Gwalior State's department under Garde finding the second slab and removing it to Gwalior, restoring (1923–29) and resetting the serpent slab; a new state's list, two central and four state monuments, the palace protected by no one; spending reported at second hand; one remembered clearance; INTACH's survey of the whole town (2020–21), a list without legal force; the palace notice and the revenue order of 15 January 2021 (U7); a stolen Umā-Maheśvara and defaced sculpture; quarries, blasts, herds and a cracking repair on the hill, leading to the people of Chapter 12.
through_lines.12: Udaypur at the last record (early 2020s): the census's slow village (1901 928 or 1,619; 1971 2,025; 2011 6,383); the state's village of panchayat, two 'nearest' stations and schools (record of services stops 1979); households in the ruins; wheat for the Ganj Basoda mandi, district crafts, quarry wages, fields against the reserved forest; the living hill of bats, vultures, herds, pilgrims and trekkers, and the 1968 Udaipura block (not shown to be this hill); visitors who take darśan and leave, officials' VIP darśan; the town becoming visible in 2021 (walkers, Saxena's film, Bhopal); residents setting back their own shopfronts in 2021; outsiders' verdicts, each attributed, the record speaking about residents more than for them; expectations of a tourist town, where the arc from a king's town to a visited village reaches the present, into the Afterword.
through_lines.13: Afterword: the record's horizon (the 2019 letter; 2021 in a clause each; Vivek's post of 20 February 2022 the latest dated item; the survey 2021 or later, RR-31); protection building by building and no one answering for the town; the proposals on record from translations on site, guides and walks, clearing and monitoring, schools, residents and merchants, readers of inscriptions and the book's open questions, to circuits, partnership and Mishra's heritage town, each attributed; the proposals tested 'on the evidence of this book' (who pays, where the risk is, pace, people); the one argument, 'this book argues', conservation by use; the close on the temple seen from the Ganj Basoda road and the lane its residents widened.
through_lines.2: The land the founder found: a river country whose river does not reach the town, a sandstone hill, one wet season, black soil, thin forest, water that had to be made and a seam of stone; the setting, never the cause.
through_lines.3: What stood in Udaypur's country before Udaypur, told for what it means to Udaypur: old names, Vidisha in literature and excavation (the Gazetteer capped at 40% a unit), its dynasties, roads and shrines, Gupta caves near the town, the move to Bhilsa and its Sun god, and the eighth-to-tenth-century frontier on Udaypur's range; who held the hill stays open.
through_lines.4: The Paramāras as a polity, from the fire-born legend first told on Udaypur's stone to Udayāditya's recovery of Malwa, his descent, reign and family; 1080 firm and 1059 a reading; the practice of royal temple-building and the treatise ideal of the town; and Udayapura in its records and in testimony, ending on the Udayeśvara as the one dated royal work.
through_lines.5: The Udayeśvara read as historical evidence: the type and the building as it stands, with its vedī and court; the Bhūmija tower, its disputed origin, its place among Paramāra temples and between Khajuraho and the Deccan; the craft of its surfaces and the guilds behind them; the image programme set by rule and adjusted for symmetry; its damage; the texts as norms; Śaiva Siddhānta and the readings laid on the temple, ending on the temple's own inscribed words (Ch 6).
through_lines.6: Udaypur's inscriptions as evidence of literate royal culture: the signed six lines of 1080; the faulty V.S. 1116 inscription kept apart (held, RR-1); Amērā's dated verse; the praśasti as object, self-portrait, genealogy and claimed conquests, and its lost maker; the serpent of letters and its fellows, Dhārā's halls, Bhoja's books and the courts' poets; the dating of letters; the porch archive under Caulukya then Paramāra masters; the last Paramāra traces; Persian from 1336; the hill's pilgrims and unread lines; the limits of the record, into Chapter 7.
through_lines.7: Udaypur's wider built heritage as evidence for its history, not an inventory: the counted monuments and blanket survey dates; the nameless hill wall (Beglar's account held, RR-15), its interior, its dating proposals and the untried lichen method; Bhoja's treatise on forts against the bastions; the hill's Jain cave, rock panels and unfinished colossus; the walled town, its gates, palace and Mughal governor's mansion kept apart; lanes, reused houses, the Bijamandal (not Vidisha's), the Barakhambi and the Pisanhārī legend; later Hindu shrines and Jain and memorial stones; the mosques of 1336–38, 1488 and 1632 as dated marks of Delhi, Mandu and the Mughals; undated dargahs and graves; water on the hill and in the town; the Udaysagar not shown to be the Udayasamudra; the older Bhujariya; Vikrama's tank at Amērā as water given for merit, leading into Chapter 8's gifts.
through_lines.8: Gifts, not a budget: three dated gifts at Udaypur (1163 to Udaleśvara, Ganguly only, RR-17; early 1170s, Lūṇapasāka's village to Vaidyanātha; 1229, Dhāmadeva's four biswa to the Udayeśvara), under Caulukya then Paramāra masters (U1), and no founding endowment; the kingdom's pattern of endowment, labelled; merit and the temple as institution (Temple Economics comparative only); the hala and the water-wheel in the grants; the kundies (RR-18), the treatises' four builders, Malwa's cloth; markets, imposts and the dramma, Udayāditya's gold; the modern district's farming and trades; what worship required, the Śaiva schools and monasteries, gods beside Śiva; the drum-stone and the time-keepers' claim; the living temple, into Chapter 9.
through_lines.9: A town that narrates itself: neighbours in a lane and the district census (no counts for Udaypur); a family's claim of Paramāra descent and the Bagdi tradition as family and community memory (legal review); the ranked society and migrant Brāhmaṇas of the grants, regional; the district's languages, the village's speech undocumented, the languages of the stones; the Śivarātri fair, the Bhujariya rites, the court's festivals known from books, dress, food and the rāī; three foundings in the stories and tales told elsewhere; Berni Mata's versions growing; Bhoja the region's folk king against Udayāditya's town; the gaḍhī's threads, treasure and deserted Daulatpur, into Chapter 10.
